lines.note: Continues the preceding page's caminho da virtude, the path of virtue. The new example begins hito no ki ni toriiru, gaining someone's favour; the verb is divided over the next row without a visible terminal hyphen here.
Iru completes toriiru. The Portuguese gives pleasing someone greatly, explaining the interpersonal sense of the preceding expression.

Torimagirakasu describes mixing or confusing things. The printed abbreviated principal form ita is retained as historical inflectional evidence. Emburulhar is the historical Portuguese spelling, and the alternative gloss continues below.

runs.text: miſturar hũa couſa com outra demaneira que ſe

lines.note: The objects are mixed with one another in such a manner that they cannot be distinguished. The printed demaneira is retained as one visible sequence.
Completes the negative result clause: the things cannot be told apart. This short continuation closes the torimagirakasu definition.
Torimagire describes being very occupied or distracted. The Portuguese occupa- continues into ocupado on the next row.

runs.text: do, ou depreßa, & embaraçado com diuerſas

lines.note: Do completes occupado. The gloss connects haste and being encumbered by various matters; depreßa is preserved as printed rather than expanded or modernized.
Cousas completes the reference to being distracted or burdened with various things. It is a separate physical continuation, not a new entry.
Torimajiye means mixing with the hands. The historical jiye spelling and the printed nasal mark in mãos are retained.
Torimaki is encircling with people or troops. The historical abbreviated principal parts u and ita are retained; Vt introduces the fortress example on the following row.
Shiro wo torimaku is surrounding a fortress. The scan shows r in Xirouo, agreeing with fortaleza; the OCR Xitouo would misidentify the object.
Torimawashi is given the same encircling sense as torimaki. The printed principal-part ending ita is preserved without importing another entry's historical inflection.
The noun torimawashi concerns managing or handling something. Ca- begins kano, the demonstrative in the following example.

runs.text: no fitono torimauaxiga fayai, l, voſoi.

lines.note: Kano hito no torimawashi ga hayai, alternatively osoi, contrasts quick and slow handling of affairs. Latin l introduces the alternative and is not Japanese.

runs.text: Aquelle homem he diligente, & expedito no

lines.note: The first alternative describes that person as diligent and efficient. The scan supplies the i missing from the OCR dilgente, yielding diligente.

runs.text: meneo das couſas, &c. ou tardo, & atado.

lines.note: Completes the contrast: efficient in managing things, or slow and hampered. The second description translates the alternative voſoi rather than a separate entry.
The noun torimidashi is being occupied or encumbered. The Portuguese description continues into embaraçado on the next physical row.

Iroiro no torimidashi ga atte means having various occupations or distractions. The headword and visible m support torimidaxiga against OCR torinidaxiga; the faint italic capital in Tẽ- begins tendo below.
Tẽ- plus do forms tendo, having various occupations and encumbrances. The tilde abbreviation is retained rather than expanded in the transcription.
The verb torimidasu means confusing or disrupting something. The printed aita is a historical abbreviated past form, and per- begins perturbar below.

runs.text: turbar algũa couſa. ¶ Item, Estar muito

lines.note: Turbar completes perturbar, disturbing something. A second sense then begins: being very occupied, specified as business on the next row.
The second sense is being occupied with affairs. Moshimo starts the conditional example, and tori- is the first part of torimidasu.
Moshimo torimidasu koto mo araba expresses the possibility of being occupied or distracted. The Portuguese conditional begins se por ventura and divides estiver across this row and the next.
Completes estiver ocupado ou impedido: if one happens to be occupied or hindered. It belongs to the conditional example, not the following birdlime entry.

runs.text: Viſco de tomar paßaros: às vezes

lines.note: Torimochi is birdlime used to catch birds. The gloss begins a note that the shorter form mochi is also used.
Completes the usage note: it is sometimes called simply Mochi. This Japanese word is embedded in a Portuguese explanation and is a typeface-review term.

runs.text: Torimochi, tçu, otta.i, Torifayaſu. l, Chi

lines.note: The hospitality sense of torimochi is equated with torihayasu and chisoo suru. The latter Japanese synonym is divided after Chi without a visible terminal hyphen; the mark after explanatory i is a comma.

Completes chisoo suru, providing hospitality or a welcome. The damaged Portuguese noun is read as agaſalhado, supported by the clearer repetition on the following row; the OCR inserted an extra o and space.
This noun torimochi is hospitality and favour. The Portuguese h and following letters, though partly abraded, support Agaſalhado rather than the OCR Agaſahado.
A distinct verb sense is carrying or holding in the hands. The principal parts remain those printed, and mãos completes the Portuguese phrase below.

Tegotoni raſsocuuo torimo- describes holding a candle in each hand. Rassoku is a historical candle word; NINJAL’s full lexical index identifies Rassocu. at f414 (207c13). The visible uo is the object particle, correcting OCR uno, and torimo- continues into torimotçu below.
Tçu completes torimotçu, holding. The Portuguese explicitly says to have a candle in each hand, clarifying the damaged Japanese example above.
Torimusubi, torimusubu, torimusunda means linking or tying together. The scan shows unda, not OCR runda, as the abbreviated past form.
Completes tying one thing to another, then marks a figurative use. Caxxen begins kassen, battle, with a printed terminal hyphen before its particle on the next row.

Kassen wo torimusubu means joining battle, as the Portuguese trauar peleja confirms. Enlarged letter counting supports torimuſubu against OCR toiamuſubu; the r/i region remains damaged, so this chosen reading carries a nonblocking caveat.
Batalha completes dar batalha, giving battle. This short physical row closes the figurative example.
Torinaoshi means correcting or taking something anew. The printed abbreviated principal form oita is retained, and the Portuguese second alternative continues with changing one's hold.

runs.text: a couſa na mão doutra maneira do que atinha.

lines.note: The object is taken in the hand in a different way from before. The source's atinha spacing is retained rather than regularized to modern orthography.
Kaji wo torinaosu is changing the helm or steering. The Portuguese explains turning a vessel toward another side, completed below.

runs.text: bordo a embarcação. Item, permet. Mudar o

lines.note: Completes the nautical example by turning the vessel onto another tack. A figurative extension then begins, changing one's manner or state of life.
Completes the figurative sense: changing one's manner or state of life. The rounded second letter supports modo rather than OCR mado.
The verb torinasu concerns speaking favourably, pleading, or interceding. The Portuguese bem has b, not OCR h; historical arrezoar and the printed principal form ita are retained.
The alternative interceder explicitly gives intercession as a sense of the verb above. It closes that entry before the related noun.
The noun torinashi is intercession. The partly abraded middle of Interceſão appears to show one long s; no doubling has been supplied merely from the expected Portuguese spelling.
Torinashite names the person who intercedes. The final -te identifies the agent, while the Portuguese gives intercessor.
Torinobe, torinoburu, torinobeta means taking and extending something. The explanatory i introduces making it long on the next row.

Completes the gloss as making something long. The example begins taking the naginata farther along its shaft; the visible spelling Nagunatauo is retained rather than normalized, and a word space separates it from tori-.

runs.text: Tomar a alabarda pollo cabo, ou

lines.note: Noburu completes the example tori-noburu across the column boundary. The Portuguese describes taking the halberd by the end of its shaft, with a second position below.

runs.text: mais por baixo. ¶ Item, Dilatar as couſas, ou

lines.note: The implement may be grasped farther down. A second sense of torinoburu is then introduced: delaying or prolonging matters.
Mono wo torinoburu hito ja describes someone who delays things. The visible terminal dash after fito- is preserved as a physical division before gia.

runs.text: He homem vagaroſo, ou que dilata

lines.note: Gia completes the Japanese copular phrase. The Portuguese characterizes the person as slow or one who postpones things.
Completes the description of delaying matters greatly. This short row closes the example before the separate climbing verb.
Torinobori, torinoboru, torinobotta means going up or ascending. The example begins shiro e, to the fortress.
Shiro e torinoboru is ascending to the fortress; the alternative gloss begins entering it, with force specified next. The abraded opening letters agree with the clearly printed headword.
Completes entering by force, then gives yama e torinoboru, climbing a mountain. The Portuguese b is visible in Subir, correcting OCR Sulir.
Ao monte completes the translation of yama e torinoboru, ascending the mountain. It is a short physical continuation of the previous example.
Torinoko is a kind of paper, identified simply as paper of that name. The worn middle letters support chamado; the OCR charmado inserts an extra r.

The gloss names a blacksmith's tongs. The scan is read literally as Torino axi; an expected f before axi is not securely present in this impression, so it has not been supplied. NINJAL's Torinofaxi provides lexical context, not authority to restore missing ink.

Torinomi describes drinking heavily or without order. Preserve the visible circumflex in the printed abbreviated principal form ôda rather than expanding or modernizing the inflection in the transcription.

Torinoke means removing or setting aside. The worn final Portuguese word is provisionally read afatar: one tall crossbarred shaft is visible after afa-. A damaged st or ſt ligature could instead yield expected afastar, but the low s element is not securely established even against the following Afaſtarſe.
Torinoki is withdrawing or moving away. The gloss continues tornar atras, turning back; the r/n sequence supports tornar rather than OCR tomar, while the printed principal form oita is retained.
Completes turning back in war. The printed naguerra remains joined, and the military context distinguishes withdrawal from ordinary removal.
Torinori denotes many people boarding together. The repeated t in otta and the Portuguese Embarcaremſe are visible despite abrasion, correcting OCR oita and Embartar enſe.
Another sense is many people mounting horses. Uma ni begins the example, and the visible terminal hyphen is retained even though it falls between the particle and the following verb.
Completes uma ni torinoru, mounting horses together. This short Japanese continuation is a real body row.
Torinose is boarding or causing others to board. The principal form ſuru is retained as printed, and the nasal abbreviation in ẽ- begins embarcar below.
Barcar completes the divided Portuguese embarcar. Its nasal material is represented by the preceding tilde rather than an added m in this row.

runs.text: Cabeça, ou principal em algum officio

lines.note: Tooryoo is the head or principal practitioner of a craft. The first vowel bears a circumflex and the final vowel a caron; these different marks are preserved.

The definition singles out carpenters and begins a note on use in either a good or bad sense. The scan supports particularmete: no secure n or abbreviation tilde is supplied in its worn middle. The unusual im before bonam is retained.
Completes the Latin usage phrase, in a good and in a bad sense. Nusubito no introduces the adverse example involving thieves; the visible u corrects OCR Noſubitono.

Nusubito no tooryoo is the chief of thieves. The Portuguese reads Cabeça de ladroes, replacing the OCR's garbled dedaorcos. The area over the vowels is worn, and no secure nasal mark has been supplied.
Torikeshi is extinguishing a fire or candle. The printed abbreviated past form eita is retained rather than regularized from modern morphology.
The figurative example is shiro wo torikesu, extinguishing a fortress. Per met. explicitly signals that this is an extension of the preceding literal sense.

runs.text: Aſolar, ou deſtruir de todo a fortaleza, &

lines.note: The figurative gloss means laying waste to or wholly destroying the fortress. Its people are included on the next physical row.
Gente della completes the destruction of the fortress and its people. This closes the figurative example rather than beginning the following horticultural entry.

runs.text: Ramo de aruore, ou de vide, &c.

lines.note: Toriki concerns a branch of a tree or vine used in layering. The visible c in the final abbreviation restores &c. rather than OCR &.
Mergulhado describes the branch as laid into the ground. Toriki wo suru is performing this layering, and the following Portuguese infinitive is Mergulhar, not OCR Mergulhas.

runs.text: ou enterrar algum ramo pera que crie raizes

lines.note: The branch is buried so that it develops roots. The visible letters give enterrar and plural raizes, correcting OCR enternar and raizo without adding a modern accent.

runs.text: na terra, & ſe poßa traſplantar, ou fazer ou-

lines.note: The roots develop in the earth so that the branch can be transplanted or form another tree. This is an indented continuation, and ou- begins outra on the next row.
Tra completes outra: another tree beside the parent plant. The source uses mãy, mother, to describe the original tree in this layering process.
Torikirame describes doing something with conspicuous display or splendour. The Portuguese manner phrase continues below.

runs.text: fauſto, & aparato, ou com outro concerto como

lines.note: The activity is performed with pomp and display or with another arrangement. The visible m supports como, correcting OCR cono; the examples follow on the next row.

runs.text: de conuite, atauio, &c, mais luſtroſamente do

lines.note: Feasting and adornment exemplify the showy arrangement, done more splendidly than usual. The comparison continues into custumado below.
Completes do custumado, than what is customary. This short continuation closes the description of unusual splendour.
Torikirameki is assigned the same sense of splendid display. The supplied eita principal form remains literal rather than being regularized from another verb.
Torikise is putting an additional garment or covering on someone. The initial T and final mais are visible, correcting OCR roriqixe and mair.

runs.text: veſtila, ou cubrir com ella a outro.

lines.note: The extra item is put on another person or used to cover them. Historical cubrir and the object form vestila remain as printed.
Torisata is current talk or report. The repeated Toriſata begins the example and corrects OCR Tonſata; it is not a different Japanese word.

runs.text: Falar, ou tratar das couſas que cor-

lines.note: Torisata suru means talking about or discussing matters that are current. The divided Portuguese cor- continues into correm on the next row.
Rem completes correm, literally things that are circulating. This closes the explanation of current talk.

runs.text: Oque toma paſſaros com cana enuis-

lines.note: Torisashi is someone who catches birds with a cane coated in birdlime. The final enuis- continues as enviscada; the worn letters are kept provisionally without modernizing u to v.
Cada completes the description of the cane as coated at its tip. The visible n gives na ponta, correcting OCR ma ponta.
Torisaye concerns preventing or separating people. The readable historical principal forms uru and eta replace OCR uiu and ota, without imposing a modern verb ending.

runs.text: que pelejão, ou ao que quer caſtigar, &c.

lines.note: Those fighting are separated, or someone intending to punish is restrained. The visible middle letters support pelejão, correcting OCR pelção.

The damaged catchword is provisionally read Toriſoro-, anticipating the next page's Torisoroye. The internal ſ/o remains abraded; the clear terminal o and hyphen are retained.
